title: Wavelength-Selective control of Atomic Scale Au Contacts
authors: Werner Brämer-Escamilla, Floralba Lopez, Laila Procel, David Llerena, Carlos Sabater, Ernesto Medina
abstract: We demonstrate wavelength-selective control of atomic motion in a mechanically controllable Au break junction. Excitation at $λ_{\mathrm{form}}\simeq 530~{\rm nm}$ drives gap closure and metallic bridge formation, whereas excitation at $λ_{\mathrm{rup}}\simeq 407~{\rm nm}$ drives neck thinning, bridge rupture, and subsequent gap opening. Unlike conventional optical switching in metallic contacts, where illumination primarily acts via thermal expansion, the present experiment reveals oppositely directed atomic drift at different wavelengths. Time-resolved conductance traces allow us to distinguish two dynamical regimes. In the tunneling regime, exponential conductance transients measure the drift velocity of the gap coordinate for both gap closure and gap opening. In the metallic regime, the Sharvin relation converts linear $\sqrt{G/G_0}$ transients into radial neck-growth and neck-thinning velocities of comparable magnitude. These results establish optically selected atomic drift as a mechanism for reversible control of metallic nanocontacts and provide a quantitative route to follow plasmon-assisted atomic rearrangements in real time.
summary: The researchers achieved wavelength-selective control over the movement of atoms in gold nanocontacts using laser illumination. By comparing conductance changes under green versus blue light, they showed that different wavelengths drive opposite atomic drifts—one promoting bridge formation and the other promoting rupture. This establishes a new mechanism for reversibly controlling metallic contacts at the atomic scale.
main_problem: To demonstrate wavelength-selective control over atomic motion (drift) within metallic nanocontacts, moving beyond simple thermal switching mechanisms.
main_result: Illumination at different wavelengths drives opposite and distinct atomic rearrangements—gap closure/growth with green light ($\lambda \simeq 530$ nm) versus neck thinning/rupture with blue light ($\lambda \simeq 407$ nm).
method: Time-resolved conductance measurements are performed on a mechanically controllable Au break junction, analyzing dynamics in both the tunneling and metallic regimes.
model_or_system: The system is an atomic-scale gold contact (Au nanogap) studied under ambient conditions. The analysis uses established models for conductance decay (exponential in tunneling regime) and linear growth ($\sqrt{G}$ vs time in metallic regime).
key_observables: Conductance ($G$) vs Time, gap closing/opening velocities ($v_f, v_b$), and radial neck-growth/thinning velocities ($v_r$).
important_parameters: Wavelengths ($\lambda_{	ext{form}} \simeq 530$ nm for formation; $\lambda_{	ext{rup}} \simeq 407$ nm for rupture); the quantum conductance unit ($G_0$).
main_assumptions: The observed reversal of motion is attributed to a wavelength-dependent modification of the effective free-energy landscape, rather than uniform heating.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate conductance dynamics showing exponential transients during gap closure/opening and linear $\sqrt{G}$ vs time plots demonstrating growth (green light) or thinning (blue light).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the experimental setup using an MCBJ, details measurements in both tunneling and metallic regimes, presents evidence for wavelength-dependent drift rates, and concludes by modeling this control via modified activation barriers.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean, measurable platform to study non-equilibrium atomic dynamics driven by light, which has implications for understanding energy dissipation and directed transport in nanoscale quantum devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Diagrammatic representation of the experimental setup. The distance between the contacts on the neck of the gold wire is controlled by a piezoelectric element, which is con- nected to a function generator via a piezoelectric controller. Both the conductance measurements and the switching of the lasers on and off are controlled by a computer via a DAQ (Data Acquisition Unit).

FIG. 2. Experimental results for the conductance of a) an initially formed metallic bridge that is ruptured by the blue wavelength laser and b) an initially open gap, in which a metallic bridge is formed by the green wavelength laser. The black sequence of square pulses shows the junction conductance, while the blue (online) and yellow (online) represent laser pulses on the junction.

Figure 2 shows the conductance dynamics for light- induced bridge rupture and bridge formation. In both protocols, up to 20 laser pulses are applied sequentially. Panel (a) shows that blue illumination ruptures a pre- existing metallic bridge: the conductance drops when the blue laser is turned on, and the bridge reforms after the laser is turned off. Panel (b) shows the complementary process: starting from an open gap, green illumination forms a metallic bridge, which ruptures again after the laser is turned off.
